extracted.intended_audience: distance-education administrators, librarians, instructional designers, and e-learning support staff
extracted.subtask_short: designing call centres and virtual library support
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, implementing, and evaluating call-centre services and virtual library support for e-learners in higher education. Covers organizational framing, service design, technology, staffing, and pedagogical alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational & professional framing for change
rubrics_metrics.description: When attempting to implement a call centre, senior administration must demonstrate how its implementation is (a) consistent with the culture and values of the organization, (b) consistent with academics’ professional values, and (c) in the best interest of the students and organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major change requires that changes be framed properly in order for them to be accepted (Garvin & Roberto, 2005; Reger et al., 1994). Carefully framing the issue in terms of fundamental organizational and professional values, and clearly outlining advantages to students, academics, and the institution, will be essential for successful implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with distance-education foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: Distance education should be built on two foundations: the needs of the intended students, and the learning outcomes of the course or program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifts the education model from campus-centric to student-centred; services (e.g., call centres) should be designed to support students' needs and achieve learning outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide immediate, appropriate responses to student inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Students typically want immediate answers to their inquiries, most of which can be accommodated by the call centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When combined with team teaching and an electronic bulletin board, call centres can meet demands of students requiring flexibility and timely academic support handled quickly, efficiently, and by the right person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear distinction between academic vs administrative inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: There needs to be a clear understanding of what is and is not an academic inquiry, so that academics and tutors do not feel threatened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By making a clear distinction, the integrity of the educational experience is maintained and academics can be reassured about the nature of inquiries handled by the call centre versus those escalated to academics/tutors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use call centres to eliminate routine administrative load
rubrics_metrics.description: Elimination of tedious administrative inquiries, for which academics and tutors typically have little or no interest and/or training, should be appealing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freeing academics from routine administration allows them to focus on thoughtful interactions with students; savings can be redirected to course design that increases meaningful interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage savings to increase meaningful student-academic interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: If savings gained from implementing a call centre are used to encourage course designs that increase meaningful interaction, the model is particularly appealing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More meaningful interaction adds value to the course and helps counter criticism that distance education has little student-academic interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use CRM/analytics to inform course improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: CRM software could provide academics with valuable insights by gathering student inquiries on certain courses into a single location for analysis, a feature valuable for course re-writes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When many people develop and deliver a course in a distributed environment, CRM software can be particularly helpful for identifying recurring student issues and informing revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce student isolation and improve institutional relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: A single, instant source of support can reduce student frustration and help build the relationship between the student and the institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improved service in obtaining timely academic assistance may improve completion rates and student retention; institutions can proactively manage student relationships to ensure needs are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design engaging, high-involvement call-centre jobs
rubrics_metrics.description: By utilizing high-involvement human-resource practices, meaningful and engaging jobs can be designed that hold the potential to improve user satisfaction and reduce employee absenteeism and turnover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Job design and HR practices matter for service quality and staff retention in call centres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and manage resistance to call-centre adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to implement a call centre in distance education will likely meet some resistance; proponents should strive to develop a value-added model and be cognizant of criticisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful communication, framing in organizational/professional values, and outlining clear benefits to stakeholders are essential strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability and role expansion potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Over time, roles and responsibilities of a call centre could expand, and with sufficient economies of scale, might even be able to provide direct academic support rather than just escalate academic inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for possible role evolution and economies of scale when designing services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable and personalized library services for e-learners
rubrics_metrics.description: Distance learners frequently do not have direct access to full range of library services and materials; this necessitates equitable services that are more personalized than might be expected on campus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow professional guidelines (Canadian Library Association; ACRL) to ensure parity of access and personalization for remote learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Librarians' role shift to educator and facilitator
rubrics_metrics.description: Librarians must assert themselves as key players in the learning process, changing roles from information providers to educators; they have become providers of technical support and transformed from 'information gatekeepers' to 'information gateways'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Involvement as teachers and learners in learning communities helps shift focus from explaining resources to meeting ongoing information needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and hybrid nature of the virtual library
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtual library: remote access to contents and services, combining an on-site collection of current/heavily used materials with an electronic network providing access to external worldwide information sources; many libraries are hybrids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design virtual services to integrate with physical collections and consider hybrid service models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help e-learners manage information abundance
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtual libraries should rescue e-learners from information overload and foster competencies and critical reflection needed to navigate an environment characterized by abundance and multiple formats/voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection, organization, and instructional support are critical services in the digital environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive resource linking and anytime/anywhere access
rubrics_metrics.description: A virtual library should link e-learners to catalogues, licensed journal databases, electronic book collections, selected Internet resources, electronic course reserves, tutorials, and opportunities for communication and interaction with librarians; permit access anytime and anywhere an Internet connection is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure seamless discovery and delivery of a range of digital and physical resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrated web-portal and catalogue search experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Libraries should develop an integrated approach with a library web site functioning as an information portal and entry point, with the catalogue and journal databases as key components; online catalogues should integrate electronic books and journals enabling one-search discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also provide user services online (check due dates, renew, request materials) to reduce barriers for remote users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use federated search and customized discovery tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Federated search tools allow users to search multiple electronic resources simultaneously using one interface; libraries can customize the tool to search a given set of resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federated search offers faster, easier searching and helps identify the most suitable databases as a research starting point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure seamless access via link-resolvers and library-link programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Link-resolving software (e.g., SFX, WebBridge) and programs like Google Scholar’s Library Links allow users to link from citations to full text and pass authentication information between databases to reduce extra logins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If open-url items are unavailable, link resolvers should direct users to catalogues and A–Z serials lists; this is especially important for internationally based online learners who need immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide personalized digital library workspaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Personalized digital libraries streamline access to frequently used resources and create a friendlier online environment by permitting users to build their own digital collections in a personal workspace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalization can be course-based and can help librarians study usage patterns to inform collection management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt Web 2.0 tools (blogs, social bookmarking, tagging) to enhance services
rubrics_metrics.description: Weblogs, social bookmarking, wikis, and other Web 2.0 tools are used for professional development, patron updates, instruction, and for allowing users to tag/classify/share resources (folksonomy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tagging and annotations can increase pedagogical benefits; vendors are beginning to integrate tagging into catalogs (e.g., PennTags, Encore).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement electronic course reserves (e-reserves)
rubrics_metrics.description: E-reserves make available, through the Web, items that faculty have selected for students in a course and can include readings, chat rooms, and bulletin boards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems may be commercial or in-house (e.g., Docutek, DRR); scanning hardcopy requires copyright permissions; include diverse digital formats (video, audio, simulations) to support varied learning objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage remote access, authentication, and technical support
rubrics_metrics.description: Managing remote access/authentication is a significant area; librarians must respond to login/password issues, browser configuration, software installation, and troubleshooting needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure front-line library staff are adequately trained, provide clear website instructions, and coordinate support with computing services; access problems must be resolved quickly to avoid frustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer multiple contact channels for e-learners
rubrics_metrics.description: E-learners benefit from having a variety of means to contact the library, including email, web forms, and a toll-free telephone number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple channels increase accessibility and learner connectedness to library support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design email reference services with awareness of trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Email reference provides around-the-clock accessibility, a written record, transmission of search results, and time for librarians to reflect; however, the absence of verbal and non-verbal cues can impair the reference interview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Service designers should weigh the benefits of asynchronous email against the need for richer interaction and consider augmenting email with other synchronous or mediated reference options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for inequalities in access and maintain print-delivery solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to bear in mind inequalities such as access to computing equipment, Internet speed/stability, and information skills; not all needed resources are available electronically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain access to print collections, provide delivery options for non-digital formats (mail, courier, designated site collections), and negotiate consortial agreements for sharing resources.
